questions.stem: The inspiratory reserve volume is best defined as the volume of air that can be

options.label: A
options.text: inspired by maximal effort over and above a normal tidal inspiration

options.label: B
options.text: expired by maximal effort after a normal tidal expiration

options.label: C
options.text: left in the lung after a maximal expiratory effort

options.label: D
options.text: moved in and out of the lung during quiet breathing

options.label: E
options.text: inspired and expired during one full forced breath

questions.why: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional volume that can be inhaled maximally after an ordinary tidal inspiration. It represents the inspiratory capacity remaining above the end of a normal inhalation.

notes.B: Extra air exhaled after a normal tidal expiration defines expiratory reserve volume, rather than an additional inspiratory volume.
notes.C: Air remaining after maximal expiration defines residual volume, which cannot be expelled during an ordinary spirometric manoeuvre.
notes.D: The volume inhaled or exhaled during quiet breathing is tidal volume, rather than the additional inspiratory reserve.
notes.E: The maximal volume moved between full inspiration and full expiration is vital capacity, which includes several component lung volumes.

questions.stem: Functional residual capacity is the sum of the

options.label: A
options.text: vital capacity and the residual volume

options.label: B
options.text: expiratory reserve volume and the residual volume

options.label: C
options.text: tidal volume and the inspiratory reserve volume

options.label: D
options.text: inspiratory reserve volume and the residual volume

options.label: E
options.text: tidal volume and the expiratory reserve volume

questions.why: Functional residual capacity is the volume remaining in the lungs at the end of passive tidal expiration. It combines the expiratory reserve volume with residual volume, reflecting the resting balance of lung and chest wall recoil.

notes.A: Vital capacity plus residual volume equals total lung capacity, the lung volume after a maximal inspiration.
notes.C: Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume equals inspiratory capacity, measured from the end of quiet expiration to maximal inspiration.
notes.D: Inspiratory reserve volume and residual volume describe opposite extremes of lung volume and do not combine to define functional residual capacity.
notes.E: Tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume omits residual volume, which forms part of the gas remaining after quiet expiration.

questions.stem: Inspiratory capacity is made up of the

options.label: A
options.text: residual volume plus the expiratory reserve volume

options.label: B
options.text: inspiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume

options.label: C
options.text: tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve volume

options.label: D
options.text: tidal volume plus the expiratory reserve volume

options.label: E
options.text: vital capacity minus the tidal volume

questions.why: Inspiratory capacity is the maximum volume that can be inhaled starting at the end of a normal tidal expiration. It therefore includes one tidal inspiration and the additional inspiratory reserve volume above it.

notes.A: Residual volume plus expiratory reserve volume equals functional residual capacity, the volume already present before the inspiratory manoeuvre begins.
notes.B: Inspiratory reserve volume does not normally include residual volume, which remains in the lungs after maximal expiration.
notes.D: Tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume includes a reserve below the starting expiratory level, rather than the full inspiratory reserve.
notes.E: Subtracting tidal volume from vital capacity leaves both inspiratory and expiratory reserves, rather than the volume available for inspiration from resting expiration.

questions.stem: The chief reason the residual volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry is that it

options.label: A
options.text: changes with every breath the subject takes

options.label: B
options.text: is exchanged completely with each tidal breath

options.label: C
options.text: exists only during forced inspiration

options.label: D
options.text: cannot be expelled from the lung by any expiratory effort

options.label: E
options.text: is too small to register on a spirometer trace

questions.why: Simple spirometry records the volumes of gas entering or leaving the lungs through the instrument. Residual volume remains after maximal expiration and therefore requires indirect measurement, such as gas dilution or body plethysmography.

notes.A: Lung volumes can vary with physiological conditions, but ordinary breath-to-breath variation is not why residual volume cannot be recorded directly.
notes.B: Residual gas is not completely exchanged during each tidal breath; it remains within the lungs even after maximal voluntary expiration.
notes.C: Residual volume is defined at maximal expiration, not during forced inspiration, and remains inaccessible to ordinary direct spirometric measurement.
notes.E: The limitation is not insufficient instrumental sensitivity; residual gas cannot be moved out of the lungs into the spirometer.

questions.stem: A physiological role attributed to the residual volume is to

options.label: A
options.text: provide the main driving force for passive expiration

options.label: B
options.text: generate the negative intrapleural pressure at rest

options.label: C
options.text: supply the surfactant that lines the alveoli

options.label: D
options.text: match ventilation to perfusion at the lung apex

options.label: E
options.text: keep alveolar O2 and CO2 from swinging widely between breaths

questions.why: Gas retained in the lungs between breaths provides a reservoir that buffers fluctuations in alveolar gas composition. Functional residual capacity, which includes residual volume, is especially important in maintaining relatively stable alveolar oxygen and carbon dioxide tensions.

notes.A: Passive expiration is driven principally by elastic recoil of the respiratory system following inspiratory muscle relaxation, rather than by residual gas alone.
notes.B: Negative intrapleural pressure primarily reflects opposing elastic tendencies of the lungs and chest wall within the sealed pleural compartment.
notes.C: Surfactant is synthesised by type II alveolar epithelial cells, rather than being supplied by gas remaining after maximal expiration.
notes.D: Regional ventilation–perfusion matching depends on gravity, vascular and airway properties, and local regulation rather than residual volume alone.

questions.stem: Vital capacity is typically larger in a tall athletic man than in a small sedentary woman mainly because it is increased by

options.label: A
options.text: greater body size and build

options.label: B
options.text: a higher resting respiratory rate

options.label: C
options.text: a larger anatomical dead space

options.label: D
options.text: a lower pulmonary compliance

options.label: E
options.text: a reduced functional residual capacity

questions.why: Vital capacity generally increases with body and lung size, and population reference values vary with height, age and sex. Physical conditioning and respiratory muscle function can also influence measured performance, so individual comparisons are not absolute.

notes.B: Resting respiratory rate influences minute ventilation, but taking breaths more frequently does not directly increase maximal mobilisable lung volume.
notes.C: Anatomical dead space reflects conducting airway volume; a larger dead space does not itself explain a larger measured vital capacity.
notes.D: Reduced lung compliance increases the pressure required for expansion and can reduce lung volumes, as in restrictive pulmonary disease.
notes.E: A reduced functional residual capacity changes resting lung volume but does not necessarily increase the difference between total capacity and residual volume.

questions.stem: Measured vital capacity tends to fall when a subject moves from standing to lying down because

options.label: A
options.text: surfactant secretion by type II cells increases

options.label: B
options.text: abdominal contents push the diaphragm upward

options.label: C
options.text: intrapleural pressure becomes more negative

options.label: D
options.text: pulmonary blood volume falls by about 400 ml

options.label: E
options.text: airway resistance drops in the dependent regions

questions.why: When a person lies supine, abdominal contents tend to displace the diaphragm towards the thorax, reducing available lung expansion. The resulting changes in respiratory mechanics and central blood distribution may reduce measured vital capacity, particularly in susceptible individuals.

notes.A: A postural change does not principally reduce vital capacity by acutely increasing surfactant secretion, which normally helps maintain alveolar stability.
notes.C: Supine positioning generally reduces resting lung volume and alters regional pleural pressure; increased negative pressure is not the principal proposed mechanism.
notes.D: Pulmonary blood volume generally increases rather than falls when blood redistributes centrally from upright to supine posture.
notes.E: A decrease in airway resistance would facilitate airflow, rather than explain the mechanical limitation imposed by upward displacement of the diaphragm.

questions.stem: In a classic restrictive disorder such as pulmonary fibrosis, the FEV1/VC ratio is characteristically

options.label: A
options.text: unchanged with an increased total lung capacity

options.label: B
options.text: zero because no air can be forcibly expired

options.label: C
options.text: preserved or high while both FEV1 and VC are reduced

options.label: D
options.text: markedly reduced with a normal VC

options.label: E
options.text: reduced with a greatly increased residual volume

questions.why: Restrictive disease reduces total lung capacity and usually reduces both forced expiratory volume in one second and vital capacity. Because these volumes fall proportionately or vital capacity falls more, their ratio generally remains normal or rises.

notes.A: Restriction is defined by a reduced total lung capacity; increased total capacity is more suggestive of hyperinflation than pulmonary fibrosis.
notes.B: Patients with restrictive disease can usually exhale forcibly, so a reduced maximal volume does not mean the expiratory ratio becomes zero.
notes.D: A substantially reduced FEV1/VC ratio is characteristic of airflow obstruction, rather than the classic proportional volume reduction of restriction.
notes.E: Marked residual-volume elevation with a reduced expiratory ratio suggests air trapping and obstruction, not the usual spirometric pattern of pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: Lung compliance is correctly described as the

options.label: A
options.text: volume of gas crossing the membrane per mmHg per minute

options.label: B
options.text: tendency of the lung to recoil toward collapse

options.label: C
options.text: ratio of ventilation to perfusion in a lung unit

options.label: D
options.text: change in lung volume per unit change in distending pressure

options.label: E
options.text: pressure needed to drive one unit of air through the airway

questions.why: Lung compliance measures the change in lung volume produced by a change in transpulmonary distending pressure. A highly compliant lung expands more for a given pressure change, whereas a stiff lung has reduced compliance.

notes.A: Gas transfer per unit partial-pressure difference and time describes pulmonary diffusing capacity, not the mechanical distensibility of the lungs.
notes.B: Elastic recoil describes the tendency of expanded tissue to return towards a smaller volume; elastance is the reciprocal of compliance.
notes.C: Ventilation–perfusion ratio compares regional airflow with blood flow, rather than relating changes in lung volume to distending pressure.
notes.E: The pressure difference required to produce a specified airflow relates to airway resistance, rather than static lung compliance.

questions.stem: Of the following, the condition that raises lung compliance rather than lowering it is

options.label: A
options.text: pulmonary fibrosis

options.label: B
options.text: pulmonary oedema

options.label: C
options.text: kyphoscoliosis

options.label: D
options.text: bronchial obstruction

options.label: E
options.text: emphysema

questions.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and elastic support, reducing lung elastic recoil and increasing static pulmonary compliance. Although the lungs expand relatively easily, reduced recoil and airway support impair expiration and promote air trapping.

notes.A: Pulmonary fibrosis increases tissue stiffness through structural remodelling, requiring greater distending pressure for a given volume change and reducing compliance.
notes.B: Pulmonary oedema increases lung fluid content and often decreases lung compliance, making respiratory expansion more difficult.
notes.C: Kyphoscoliosis restricts chest wall movement and reduces respiratory-system compliance, rather than producing the high static lung compliance characteristic of emphysema.
notes.D: Bronchial obstruction primarily increases airway resistance and can reduce dynamic compliance; obstruction alone does not establish increased static lung compliance.

questions.stem: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine lowers alveolar surface tension chiefly to

options.label: A
options.text: prevent the smaller alveoli from collapsing

options.label: B
options.text: increase the elastic recoil of the lung

options.label: C
options.text: widen the anatomical dead space

options.label: D
options.text: raise airway resistance during expiration

options.label: E
options.text: promote diffusion of CO2 across the membrane

questions.why: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine is a major surface-active phospholipid in pulmonary surfactant. By lowering surface tension at the alveolar air–liquid interface, particularly at smaller surface areas, it reduces collapsing pressure and helps stabilise differently sized alveoli.

notes.B: Reducing surface tension decreases the surface-tension component of lung elastic recoil, rather than increasing the collapsing force.
notes.C: Anatomical dead space depends on conducting airway volume, which is not the principal target of alveolar surfactant action.
notes.D: Surfactant improves alveolar stability and reduces inflation work, rather than chiefly increasing resistance within conducting airways during expiration.
notes.E: Carbon dioxide crosses the gas-exchange barrier by diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient; alveolar stabilisation is the more direct surfactant function.

questions.stem: Besides stabilising alveoli, surfactant helps to limit pulmonary oedema because reducing surface tension

options.label: A
options.text: opens dormant capillaries at the lung base

options.label: B
options.text: lessens the inward pull drawing fluid into the alveolar space

options.label: C
options.text: increases the oncotic pressure of pulmonary capillary blood

options.label: D
options.text: raises hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary veins

options.label: E
options.text: thickens the alveolar-capillary membrane

questions.why: Lower alveolar surface tension reduces the tendency of the air–liquid interface to generate forces favouring fluid accumulation in airspaces. This supports alveolar stability, alongside low capillary filtration pressure, epithelial barrier function and active alveolar fluid clearance.

notes.A: Capillary recruitment is determined mainly by vascular pressures and perfusion conditions, rather than being the direct fluid-protective effect of surfactant.
notes.C: Plasma oncotic pressure depends chiefly on circulating proteins such as albumin, not on the phospholipids lining the alveolar airspace.
notes.D: Raised pulmonary venous pressure increases capillary hydrostatic pressure and can favour oedema, rather than explaining surfactant's protective role.
notes.E: A thicker alveolar–capillary barrier would hinder gas diffusion; surfactant acts at the air–liquid interface without requiring membrane thickening.

questions.stem: A premature newborn with respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency may be treated with

options.label: A
options.text: 100% oxygen given continuously for several days

options.label: B
options.text: hyperbaric oxygen in a pressure chamber

options.label: C
options.text: exogenous bovine surfactant and corticosteroids

options.label: D
options.text: a bronchodilator such as salbutamol alone

options.label: E
options.text: atropine to reduce airway secretions

questions.why: Replacement surfactant plus corticosteroids are used; the slide also notes antenatal corticosteroids promote maturation.

questions.stem: Of a 500 ml tidal breath, the portion that does not take part in gas exchange is about

options.label: A
options.text: 500 ml, since none reaches the alveoli at rest

options.label: B
options.text: 50 ml trapped behind closed bronchioles

options.label: C
options.text: 250 ml shunted past unventilated alveoli

options.label: D
options.text: 150 ml filling the conducting airways

options.label: E
options.text: 350 ml reaching the alveoli

questions.why: A typical resting adult tidal volume is approximately 500 mL, of which roughly 150 mL occupies conducting airways that do not perform gas exchange. The remaining approximately 350 mL contributes to alveolar ventilation, assuming negligible alveolar dead space.

notes.A: Most of an ordinary tidal breath reaches gas-exchanging regions; only a fraction occupies the conducting airway dead space.
notes.B: Anatomical dead space consists of ventilated conducting airways, not a small volume trapped exclusively behind closed bronchioles.
notes.C: A vascular shunt describes blood bypassing ventilated alveoli, rather than the volume of inspired air occupying conducting airways.
notes.E: Approximately 350 mL is the portion normally available for alveolar ventilation in this example, rather than the conducting airway dead-space volume.

questions.stem: Physiological dead space differs from anatomical dead space in that it also includes

options.label: A
options.text: the volume of the trachea and large bronchi

options.label: B
options.text: gas left in the lung after maximal expiration

options.label: C
options.text: air shunted directly from artery to vein

options.label: D
options.text: the conducting airways down to the terminal bronchioles

options.label: E
options.text: alveoli that are ventilated but not adequately perfused

questions.why: Physiological dead space combines anatomical dead space in conducting airways with alveolar dead space arising from ventilation that receives little or no effective perfusion. This additional wasted alveolar ventilation increases in conditions such as pulmonary embolism.

notes.A: The trachea and large bronchi form part of anatomical dead space already, so their gas volume does not distinguish physiological dead space.
notes.B: Residual volume is gas remaining after maximal expiration and is not synonymous with ventilation that fails to participate in gas exchange.
notes.C: A right-to-left shunt involves blood reaching arterial circulation without adequate oxygenation, whereas dead space involves ventilation without adequate perfusion.
notes.D: Conducting airways through terminal bronchioles constitute anatomical dead space; physiological dead space additionally accounts for wasted ventilation within alveolar regions.

questions.stem: Compared with the systemic circulation, pressures in the pulmonary circulation are best described as

options.label: A
options.text: low in a highly distensible system (about 24/9 mmHg)

options.label: B
options.text: high in a stiff, low-compliance system

options.label: C
options.text: equal to systemic pressures but with lower flow

options.label: D
options.text: high at the apex and low at the base when upright

options.label: E
options.text: pulsatile only during forced expiration

questions.why: Pulmonary vessels form a compliant, low-resistance circulation accommodating the full right ventricular output at much lower pressures than systemic vessels. Normal resting pulmonary arterial pressure is approximately 25/8–10 mmHg, with some variation between individuals.

notes.B: High pressure and relatively stiff resistance vessels do not characterise the normal pulmonary circulation, which is adapted to low-pressure perfusion.
notes.C: Pulmonary and systemic circuits carry approximately equal average flows, but pulmonary arterial pressures and vascular resistance are much lower.
notes.D: When upright, hydrostatic effects generally make pulmonary vascular pressures higher at the base than at the apex, not the reverse.
notes.E: Pulmonary arterial flow is pulsatile because of right ventricular ejection during ordinary breathing, rather than only during forced expiration.

questions.stem: Pulmonary capillaries are relatively protected from oedema because they have

options.label: A
options.text: active sodium pumps lining the endothelium

options.label: B
options.text: high plasma oncotic pressure with low hydrostatic pressure

options.label: C
options.text: low oncotic pressure with high hydrostatic pressure

options.label: D
options.text: a thick basement membrane resisting filtration

options.label: E
options.text: continuous lymphatic valves within the alveolar wall

questions.why: Low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure limits outward filtration, while plasma oncotic pressure opposes it. These forces, together with vascular and epithelial barrier integrity and lymphatic drainage, help prevent excess lung interstitial and alveolar fluid accumulation.

notes.A: Active sodium transport by alveolar epithelial cells assists alveolar fluid clearance, but the cited capillary protection primarily concerns hydrostatic and oncotic forces.
notes.C: High capillary hydrostatic pressure with low plasma oncotic pressure favours outward fluid movement and therefore increases the risk of pulmonary oedema.
notes.D: The blood–air barrier is normally thin to facilitate gas exchange, rather than relying on a thick basement membrane to prevent filtration.
notes.E: Pulmonary lymphatics drain interstitial fluid but do not form continuous valved channels within the alveolar gas-exchange wall itself.

questions.stem: Lying down shifts roughly 400 ml of blood into the pulmonary circulation, which illustrates that the pulmonary veins act as a

options.label: A
options.text: high-resistance throttle

options.label: B
options.text: source of surfactant

options.label: C
options.text: distensible blood reservoir

options.label: D
options.text: one-way lymphatic channel

options.label: E
options.text: site of gas exchange

questions.why: The distensible pulmonary veins can hoard blood; posture changes move about 400 ml in or out of this reservoir.

questions.stem: When upright, both ventilation and perfusion per unit lung volume are greater at the base than the apex, and the base is more expandable because its intrapleural pressure is

options.label: A
options.text: positive throughout the breathing cycle

options.label: B
options.text: equal to atmospheric pressure at end-expiration

options.label: C
options.text: unaffected by gravity in the standing subject

options.label: D
options.text: less negative, so the dependent lung is more distensible

options.label: E
options.text: more negative, holding those alveoli near full inflation

questions.why: Gravity produces a vertical pleural-pressure gradient, making pressure less negative at the dependent lung base in an upright person. Basal alveoli therefore start smaller and generally lie on a steeper portion of the pressure–volume curve, receiving greater tidal expansion.

notes.A: Pleural pressure is usually subatmospheric during quiet spontaneous breathing, so continuously positive basal pleural pressure is not the normal upright finding.
notes.B: Basal pleural pressure is generally less negative than apical pressure but remains subatmospheric at normal resting expiration.
notes.C: Gravity and lung weight generate regional differences in pleural pressure, so upright lung expansion is not mechanically uniform.
notes.E: More negative apical pleural pressure holds apical alveoli at larger resting volumes, leaving them relatively less expandable during ordinary tidal inspiration.

questions.stem: A patient with one healthy and one diseased lung is generally advised to lie

options.label: A
options.text: on the side of the diseased lung

options.label: B
options.text: flat on the back at all times

options.label: C
options.text: in a head-down position

options.label: D
options.text: sitting fully upright only

options.label: E
options.text: on the side of the good lung

questions.why: Lying on the good lung puts it in the dependent position where ventilation and perfusion are best.

questions.stem: Minute respiratory volume is calculated as

options.label: A
options.text: respiratory rate multiplied by tidal volume

options.label: B
options.text: tidal volume multiplied by vital capacity

options.label: C
options.text: alveolar ventilation plus dead space volume

options.label: D
options.text: vital capacity divided by inspiratory capacity

options.label: E
options.text: residual volume multiplied by respiratory rate

questions.why: Minute respiratory volume is the total volume of air moved into or out of the lungs per minute. Multiplying tidal volume by respiratory rate gives total minute ventilation; subtracting dead-space volume from each tidal breath gives alveolar ventilation.

notes.B: Tidal volume and vital capacity are both measured as volumes, so multiplying them does not yield a volume-per-minute ventilation rate.
notes.C: Dead-space volume is measured per breath, whereas alveolar ventilation is measured per minute; dead-space ventilation must be added to obtain total minute ventilation.
notes.D: Dividing vital capacity by inspiratory capacity gives a dimensionless volume ratio, not the total volume breathed per unit time.
notes.E: Residual volume remains after maximal expiration and is not the amount moved during each ordinary breath used to calculate minute ventilation.

questions.stem: Surfactant is produced by the alveolar cell described as

options.label: A
options.text: the bronchial goblet cell

options.label: B
options.text: the type II pneumocyte

options.label: C
options.text: the type I lining cell

options.label: D
options.text: the alveolar macrophage

options.label: E
options.text: the ciliated columnar cell

questions.why: Type II pneumocytes synthesise and secrete pulmonary surfactant from lamellar bodies onto the alveolar air–liquid interface. These cuboidal epithelial cells also proliferate after injury and can help regenerate the alveolar epithelium.

notes.A: Bronchial goblet cells secrete mucus to trap inhaled material in conducting airways, rather than producing the principal alveolar surfactant.
notes.C: Type I pneumocytes form most of the thin alveolar gas-exchange surface, whereas surfactant production is the specialised function of type II cells.
notes.D: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose inhaled particles and microorganisms, rather than functioning as the principal secretory source of pulmonary surfactant.
notes.E: Ciliated columnar cells move mucus along conducting airways and do not provide the main surfactant secretion lining alveolar airspaces.

questions.stem: The flat cell that forms most of the gas-exchange surface of the alveolus is the

options.label: A
options.text: alveolar macrophage

options.label: B
options.text: mast cell

options.label: C
options.text: type I pneumocyte

options.label: D
options.text: type II pneumocyte

options.label: E
options.text: Clara (club) cell

questions.why: Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin squamous epithelial cells covering most of the alveolar surface. Together with capillary endothelium and associated basement membranes, they minimise diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.

notes.A: Alveolar macrophages patrol alveolar surfaces and remove particulate material, but do not form the continuous thin epithelial gas-exchange barrier.
notes.B: Mast cells release inflammatory mediators such as histamine and are not the flattened epithelial cells covering most alveolar surface area.
notes.D: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells specialising in surfactant secretion and epithelial repair, and cover much less alveolar surface area.
notes.E: Club cells are non-ciliated bronchiolar secretory cells that contribute to airway protection and repair, rather than forming the main alveolar gas-exchange surface.

questions.stem: Terminal bronchioles are kept open mainly by

options.label: A
options.text: continuous tonic contraction of their smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.text: positive pressure within their lumen at all times

options.label: C
options.text: surfactant secreted along their lining

options.label: D
options.text: the distending pressures that hold the surrounding lung open

options.label: E
options.text: rings of cartilage in their walls

questions.why: Terminal bronchioles lack cartilaginous support and depend substantially on transmural distending pressure and radial traction from surrounding expanded lung tissue to remain open. Loss of elastic attachments can promote small-airway narrowing or collapse, particularly during expiration.

notes.A: Contraction of bronchiolar smooth muscle narrows the airway lumen, rather than providing the principal outward force maintaining bronchiolar patency.
notes.B: Intraluminal pressure varies during breathing and can be subatmospheric during inspiration; airway opening depends on transmural pressure and surrounding tissue support.
notes.C: Surface-active secretions may assist small-airway stability, but the principal mechanical support described here comes from distending pressures and parenchymal traction.
notes.E: Cartilage supports the trachea and larger bronchi, but terminal bronchioles characteristically lack cartilaginous rings or plates.

questions.stem: A structural feature that distinguishes the trachea and large bronchi from the bronchioles is that the former have

options.label: A
options.text: abundant smooth muscle but no cartilage

options.label: B
options.text: no epithelial lining

options.label: C
options.text: no ability to warm inspired air

options.label: D
options.text: surfactant-secreting walls

options.label: E
options.text: cartilage with only a little smooth muscle

questions.why: Tracheal cartilage rings and bronchial cartilage plates provide structural support against airway collapse. Bronchioles lack cartilage and have a proportionally prominent smooth-muscle layer, making their luminal calibre particularly sensitive to smooth-muscle tone and surrounding lung mechanics.

notes.A: Absence of cartilage with a relatively prominent smooth-muscle wall characterises bronchioles, rather than the trachea and larger bronchi.
notes.B: Both larger conducting airways and bronchioles possess an epithelial lining, although epithelial cell composition changes along the respiratory tree.
notes.C: Larger airways participate in warming, humidifying and filtering inspired air; these functions are not absent from the tracheobronchial tree.
notes.D: Alveolar type II cells are the principal source of pulmonary surfactant; surfactant secretion does not distinguish large cartilaginous airways from bronchioles.

questions.stem: Bronchoconstriction mediated by acetylcholine acts through which receptor, and is blocked by atropine?

options.label: A
options.text: muscarinic receptors

options.label: B
options.text: beta-2 adrenergic receptors

options.label: C
options.text: alpha-1 adrenergic receptors

options.label: D
options.text: nicotinic receptors

options.label: E
options.text: H2 histamine receptors

questions.why: Parasympathetic acetylcholine activates muscarinic receptors, particularly M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, increasing intracellular calcium and promoting contraction. Atropine antagonises muscarinic signalling and therefore can inhibit cholinergically mediated bronchoconstriction.

notes.B: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors activate smooth-muscle relaxation pathways and are the target of bronchodilators, rather than the receptors mediating acetylcholine-induced bronchoconstriction.
notes.C: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors commonly mediate vascular smooth-muscle contraction, whereas the conventional parasympathetic bronchoconstrictor pathway acts through muscarinic receptors.
notes.D: Nicotinic receptors mediate transmission in autonomic ganglia and at skeletal neuromuscular junctions, rather than directly mediating bronchial smooth-muscle contraction by acetylcholine.
notes.E: Histamine can cause bronchoconstriction mainly through H1 receptors; atropine specifically antagonises muscarinic rather than histamine receptor signalling.

questions.stem: Salbutamol relieves bronchospasm because it is an agonist at

options.label: A
options.text: nicotinic receptors

options.label: B
options.text: beta-2 adrenergic receptors

options.label: C
options.text: muscarinic cholinergic receptors

options.label: D
options.text: alpha-1 adrenergic receptors

options.label: E
options.text: H1 histamine receptors

questions.why: Salbutamol activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle, stimulating Gs-dependent adenylyl cyclase and increasing cAMP. This promotes smooth-muscle relaxation, reducing airway resistance and relieving reversible bronchospasm.

notes.A: Nicotinic receptors transmit cholinergic signals at autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junctions, rather than mediating salbutamol's direct bronchodilator effect.
notes.C: Muscarinic receptor activation commonly causes bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, whereas salbutamol produces relaxation through beta-2 adrenergic signalling.
notes.D: Alpha-1 receptors mainly mediate vasoconstrictor responses; salbutamol is used for its preferential agonist activity at airway beta-2 receptors.
notes.E: Histamine H1 receptor activation can promote bronchoconstriction and allergic responses, rather than providing the receptor target for salbutamol-induced airway relaxation.

questions.stem: Breathing cold air can trigger wheeze in a susceptible person because cooling of the airway tends to cause

options.label: A
options.text: an increase in compliance

options.label: B
options.text: closure of the glottis

options.label: C
options.text: bronchospasm

options.label: D
options.text: surfactant release

options.label: E
options.text: pulmonary vasodilatation

questions.why: Cold, dry inspired air can trigger bronchoconstriction in susceptible individuals, particularly during exercise. Airway water loss, changes in mucosal osmolarity and mediator release contribute to smooth-muscle narrowing, producing increased airway resistance and wheeze.

notes.A: Increased lung compliance means easier lung expansion, whereas cold-air-induced wheeze principally reflects narrowing of conducting airways and increased resistance.
notes.B: Glottic closure can produce upper-airway obstruction or stridor, but the characteristic cold-air-associated wheeze in asthma results from bronchial narrowing.
notes.D: Surfactant secretion chiefly stabilises alveolar surfaces and is not the principal mechanism generating cold-air-induced narrowing of bronchial smooth muscle.
notes.E: Pulmonary vascular dilatation affects perfusion, whereas wheeze from cold-air-triggered bronchospasm arises predominantly from altered airway calibre.

questions.stem: The sigmoid shape of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve arises because

options.label: A
options.text: oxygen oxidises the iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+ on binding

options.label: B
options.text: 2,3-DPG competes with oxygen for the haem pocket

options.label: C
options.text: the first O2 molecule binds most readily of the four

options.label: D
options.text: binding of one O2 molecule eases the binding of the next

options.label: E
options.text: each haem binds oxygen completely independently of the others

questions.why: Haemoglobin exhibits positive cooperativity because oxygen binding favours the transition from the lower-affinity tense state to the higher-affinity relaxed state. Successive oxygen molecules therefore bind more readily, producing a sigmoid oxygen saturation curve.

notes.A: Normal oxygen binding involves reversible interaction with ferrous haem iron; oxidation to ferric iron forms methaemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen normally.
notes.B: 2,3-DPG binds within the central cavity of deoxygenated haemoglobin and stabilises its low-affinity state rather than competing directly at the haem oxygen-binding pocket.
notes.C: The first oxygen molecule generally binds with the lowest affinity, with subsequent binding favoured by cooperative conformational changes in haemoglobin.
notes.E: Independent binding sites would not produce the characteristic cooperative sigmoid relationship; haemoglobin subunits interact through changes in quaternary structure.

questions.stem: The P50 of adult haemoglobin, about 26.6 mmHg, is defined as the PO2 at which haemoglobin is

options.label: A
options.text: fully saturated with oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: half dissociated into subunits

options.label: C
options.text: bound equally to O2 and CO2

options.label: D
options.text: releasing 50% of its 2,3-DPG

options.label: E
options.text: 50% saturated with oxygen

questions.why: P50 is the oxygen partial pressure at which haemoglobin is 50% saturated. Under standard adult physiological conditions it is approximately 26–27 mmHg; a higher P50 denotes lower affinity because more oxygen pressure is required for half-saturation.

notes.A: Full haemoglobin saturation occurs at much higher oxygen tensions and does not define the half-saturation pressure used as the affinity index.
notes.B: Haemoglobin can undergo conformational changes without dissociation into subunits; P50 concerns oxygen occupancy rather than separation of its globin chains.
notes.C: Oxygen and carbon dioxide interact with haemoglobin in different ways, and P50 does not describe an equal-binding point between these gases.
notes.D: 2,3-DPG influences oxygen affinity by stabilising deoxygenated haemoglobin, but P50 is not a direct measurement of 2,3-DPG release.

questions.stem: A rise in P50 (rightward shift of the dissociation curve) signifies that haemoglobin has

options.label: A
options.text: a decreased affinity, releasing O2 more readily to tissues

options.label: B
options.text: an increased affinity, holding O2 more tightly

options.label: C
options.text: lost its cooperative binding behaviour

options.label: D
options.text: been converted to methaemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: a reduced capacity to carry CO2

questions.why: A higher P50 means a greater oxygen partial pressure is needed to achieve 50% haemoglobin saturation. The rightward shift therefore indicates reduced oxygen affinity, favouring oxygen unloading at a given tissue oxygen tension.

notes.B: Increased affinity lowers the oxygen pressure required for half-saturation and shifts the dissociation curve towards the left rather than the right.
notes.C: Changes in temperature, pH or 2,3-DPG can shift the cooperative curve without abolishing haemoglobin's positive cooperative binding behaviour.
notes.D: Methaemoglobin contains ferric iron with impaired oxygen binding; a rightward shift alone does not demonstrate conversion of normal haemoglobin to this form.
notes.E: P50 measures haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, rather than directly determining its capacity to carry carbon dioxide as bicarbonate or carbamino compounds.

questions.stem: During exercise the oxyhaemoglobin curve shifts to the right, which is useful because it

options.label: A
options.text: abolishes the Bohr effect in working muscle

options.label: B
options.text: raises the PO2 at which O2 is delivered to active tissue

options.label: C
options.text: increases the total oxygen-carrying capacity of blood

options.label: D
options.text: allows haemoglobin to pick up more O2 in the lungs

options.label: E
options.text: prevents any unloading of O2 until the capillary end

questions.why: Exercise increases local temperature, carbon dioxide production and hydrogen ion concentration, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve rightwards. At a given tissue oxygen tension, haemoglobin saturation is lower, allowing greater unloading and substantial oxygen delivery even before tissue oxygen tension falls markedly.

notes.A: The Bohr effect contributes to the exercise-associated rightward shift because increased carbon dioxide and acidity reduce haemoglobin oxygen affinity.
notes.C: A rightward shift alters affinity and unloading, but does not increase the maximum oxygen-binding capacity determined mainly by haemoglobin concentration.
notes.D: A rightward shift reduces oxygen affinity and can slightly oppose pulmonary loading at a given oxygen tension, rather than primarily enhancing lung uptake.
notes.E: Reduced oxygen affinity facilitates unloading along the tissue capillary, rather than preventing oxygen release until blood reaches its venous end.

questions.stem: 2,3-diphosphoglycerate lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity by binding to the

options.label: A
options.text: globin chains only after oxygenation

options.label: B
options.text: haem porphyrin ring directly

options.label: C
options.text: beta chains of the haemoglobin molecule

options.label: D
options.text: alpha chains of the haemoglobin molecule

options.label: E
options.text: iron atom at the centre of each haem

questions.why: 2,3-DPG binds electrostatically within the central cavity between beta chains of deoxygenated adult haemoglobin. This stabilises the lower-affinity tense conformation and increases the oxygen pressure required for half-saturation, promoting oxygen unloading to tissues.

notes.A: The central binding cavity is most accessible in deoxygenated haemoglobin, so 2,3-DPG preferentially binds before rather than after full oxygenation.
notes.B: The haem porphyrin ring contains the iron oxygen-binding site, whereas 2,3-DPG regulates affinity by binding between globin chains.
notes.D: The principal adult haemoglobin 2,3-DPG binding cavity lies between beta chains, rather than being formed chiefly between the alpha chains.
notes.E: The central ferrous haem iron directly binds oxygen, whereas 2,3-DPG acts allosterically through positively charged residues within the globin cavity.

questions.stem: Which set of changes all shift the oxyhaemoglobin curve to the RIGHT?

options.label: A
options.text: fall in temperature, fall in pH, rise in CO2, fall in 2,3-DPG

options.label: B
options.text: rise in temperature, rise in pH, fall in CO2, rise in 2,3-DPG

options.label: C
options.text: rise in temperature, rise in pH, rise in CO2, fall in 2,3-DPG

options.label: D
options.text: rise in temperature, fall in pH, rise in CO2, rise in 2,3-DPG

options.label: E
options.text: fall in temperature, rise in pH, fall in CO2, fall in 2,3-DPG

questions.why: Increased temperature, increased carbon dioxide, reduced pH and increased 2,3-DPG all favour lower haemoglobin oxygen affinity and a rightward dissociation-curve shift. These changes increase P50 and generally facilitate oxygen release to metabolically active tissues.

notes.A: Lower temperature and lower 2,3-DPG favour increased oxygen affinity, despite the opposing rightward influences of reduced pH and increased carbon dioxide.
notes.B: Higher pH and lower carbon dioxide favour a leftward shift, so the listed changes do not all promote reduced haemoglobin oxygen affinity.
notes.C: Higher pH and lower 2,3-DPG increase oxygen affinity, counteracting the rightward effects of higher temperature and carbon dioxide.
notes.E: Lower temperature, higher pH, lower carbon dioxide and lower 2,3-DPG all favour increased affinity and a leftward rather than rightward shift.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than maternal haemoglobin largely because it

options.label: A
options.text: binds 2,3-DPG more avidly

options.label: B
options.text: contains four beta chains

options.label: C
options.text: carries iron in the ferric state

options.label: D
options.text: has no cooperative binding

options.label: E
options.text: binds 2,3-DPG less avidly

questions.why: Fetal haemoglobin contains gamma rather than beta globin chains and binds 2,3-DPG less strongly than adult haemoglobin. Reduced stabilisation of the deoxygenated state gives fetal haemoglobin higher oxygen affinity, supporting placental oxygen transfer.

notes.A: Stronger 2,3-DPG binding would stabilise deoxygenated haemoglobin and lower oxygen affinity, opposing the fetal haemoglobin advantage during placental oxygen exchange.
notes.B: Fetal haemoglobin contains two alpha and two gamma chains, rather than four beta chains; its gamma chains contribute to weaker 2,3-DPG binding.
notes.C: Ferric haem iron forms methaemoglobin and cannot bind oxygen normally, whereas physiological fetal haemoglobin uses ferrous iron like adult haemoglobin.
notes.D: Fetal haemoglobin retains cooperative oxygen binding; its higher affinity chiefly reflects weaker 2,3-DPG interactions rather than loss of cooperativity.

questions.stem: The rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve produced when a fall in pH accompanies a rise in CO2 is known as the

options.label: A
options.text: Bohr effect

options.label: B
options.text: Haldane effect

options.label: C
options.text: chloride shift

options.label: D
options.text: Hering-Breuer reflex

options.label: E
options.text: Fick principle

questions.why: The Bohr effect describes decreased haemoglobin oxygen affinity when carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion concentrations increase. Stabilisation of lower-affinity haemoglobin favours oxygen release in metabolically active tissues and helps coordinate oxygen delivery with local metabolic demand.

notes.B: The Haldane effect describes the influence of haemoglobin oxygenation on carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion carriage, rather than the reverse influence on oxygen affinity.
notes.C: Chloride shift refers to erythrocyte bicarbonate–chloride exchange during carbon dioxide transport, rather than the acid-dependent shift in haemoglobin oxygen affinity.
notes.D: The Hering–Breuer reflex uses pulmonary stretch receptor feedback to influence breathing, rather than regulating oxygen binding through carbon dioxide and pH.
notes.E: The Fick principle relates substance uptake or release to blood flow and arteriovenous concentration difference, rather than describing haemoglobin allostery.

questions.stem: The Haldane effect, by which oxygenation of blood in the lungs promotes release of CO2, occurs because binding of O2 makes haemoglobin

options.label: A
options.text: incapable of the chloride shift

options.label: B
options.text: a stronger acid, so it releases H+ and frees CO2

options.label: C
options.text: a weaker acid that takes up more H+ and retains CO2

options.label: D
options.text: unable to form any carbamino compounds

options.label: E
options.text: more avid for 2,3-DPG in the pulmonary capillary

questions.why: Oxygenation reduces haemoglobin's capacity to buffer hydrogen ions and carry carbamino carbon dioxide. Released hydrogen ions combine with bicarbonate to regenerate carbon dioxide, while carbamino compounds dissociate, facilitating pulmonary carbon dioxide elimination through the Haldane effect.

notes.A: Oxygenation does not prevent chloride shift; reverse bicarbonate–chloride exchange supports carbon dioxide regeneration within erythrocytes in pulmonary capillaries.
notes.C: Deoxygenated haemoglobin binds hydrogen ions more readily, whereas oxygenation favours their release and subsequent conversion of bicarbonate into carbon dioxide.
notes.D: Oxygenated haemoglobin has reduced carbamino binding capacity rather than becoming absolutely incapable of carrying carbon dioxide in carbamino form.
notes.E: Oxygenation reduces access to the central 2,3-DPG binding cavity; increased 2,3-DPG affinity is not the principal mechanism of carbon dioxide release.

questions.stem: During the chloride shift in systemic capillaries, chloride ions move

options.label: A
options.text: out of the red cell as oxygen moves in

options.label: B
options.text: into the plasma as carbamino compounds form

options.label: C
options.text: into the red cell as bicarbonate moves out

options.label: D
options.text: out of the red cell as bicarbonate moves out

options.label: E
options.text: into the red cell as hydrogen ions move out

questions.why: In systemic capillaries, erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase converts incoming carbon dioxide into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions. Bicarbonate exits through the band 3 anion exchanger while chloride enters, maintaining electrical neutrality during carbon dioxide uptake from tissues.

notes.A: Chloride generally leaves erythrocytes during the reverse shift in pulmonary capillaries, when bicarbonate re-enters and haemoglobin becomes oxygenated.
notes.B: Systemic carbon dioxide uptake promotes chloride entry into erythrocytes rather than chloride movement into plasma as carbamino compounds are formed.
notes.D: Bicarbonate efflux is coupled to chloride influx, so the two anions move in opposite directions through the erythrocyte exchanger.
notes.E: Hydrogen ions are buffered largely by deoxygenated haemoglobin; chloride entry is coupled to bicarbonate export rather than direct hydrogen ion transport.

questions.stem: Approximately what fraction of CO2 carried in blood travels as carbamino compounds bound to haemoglobin and plasma proteins?

options.label: A
options.text: about 1%

options.label: B
options.text: about 90%

options.label: C
options.text: about 50%

options.label: D
options.text: about 30%

options.label: E
options.text: about 70%

questions.why: Most blood carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate, with a smaller fraction carried as carbamino compounds formed on amino groups of haemoglobin and other proteins. Conventional teaching estimates carbamino transport at approximately 20–30%, depending on the accounting conditions.

notes.A: One per cent markedly underestimates the conventional contribution of carbamino compounds to total carbon dioxide transport in blood.
notes.B: Ninety per cent would make carbamino carriage overwhelmingly dominant, whereas bicarbonate formation accounts for the largest share of carbon dioxide transport.
notes.C: Half of transported carbon dioxide is greater than the usual estimate of the fraction carried as protein-bound carbamino compounds.
notes.E: Approximately 70% is commonly attributed to bicarbonate transport in teaching models, rather than the smaller carbamino contribution.

questions.stem: Myoglobin differs from haemoglobin in that each molecule

options.label: A
options.text: binds four O2 molecules cooperatively

options.label: B
options.text: releases its O2 only at high tissue PO2

options.label: C
options.text: carries oxygen in the ferric (Fe3+) state

options.label: D
options.text: lowers its affinity as O2 binds

options.label: E
options.text: binds a single O2 and has a higher affinity for it

questions.why: Myoglobin is a monomeric muscle haem protein containing one oxygen-binding haem group. Its higher oxygen affinity and hyperbolic dissociation curve allow it to retain oxygen until intracellular oxygen tension becomes sufficiently low during increased muscle demand.

notes.A: Four cooperative oxygen-binding sites characterise tetrameric haemoglobin, whereas myoglobin possesses one haem group and cannot exhibit intersubunit cooperativity.
notes.B: High oxygen tension favours myoglobin oxygen loading; its high affinity means substantial unloading occurs particularly at relatively low tissue oxygen tensions.
notes.C: Functional oxygen binding requires ferrous haem iron in both myoglobin and haemoglobin, rather than the ferric state associated with oxidised pigment.
notes.D: A single-site protein cannot show progressive cooperative affinity changes across successive oxygen-binding sites as tetrameric haemoglobin does.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide is dangerous out of proportion to small inhaled amounts because its affinity for haemoglobin is roughly

options.label: A
options.text: 200 times that of oxygen, shifting the curve left

options.label: B
options.text: one-tenth that of oxygen, shifting the curve right

options.label: C
options.text: equal to that of oxygen but it blocks 2,3-DPG

options.label: D
options.text: high only for fetal haemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: limited to the dissolved fraction of blood gas

questions.why: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin approximately 200–250 times more avidly than oxygen under typical conditions, reducing available oxygen-binding sites. It also increases oxygen affinity at remaining sites, shifting their dissociation curve leftwards and impairing tissue oxygen unloading.

notes.B: Carbon monoxide has much greater rather than lower haemoglobin affinity, and its effect on remaining oxygen-binding sites favours a leftward shift.
notes.C: Carbon monoxide competes strongly with oxygen for haem binding; its toxicity is not explained by equal affinity and isolated interference with 2,3-DPG.
notes.D: Adult as well as fetal haemoglobin can bind carbon monoxide strongly, so this mechanism is not restricted to fetal haemoglobin.
notes.E: A substantial fraction of absorbed carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin as carboxyhaemoglobin, rather than remaining only in the dissolved blood gas compartment.

questions.stem: A patient with severe carbon monoxide poisoning characteristically shows

options.label: A
options.text: pallor from true anaemia

options.label: B
options.text: a cherry-red skin colour rather than cyanosis

options.label: C
options.text: deep central cyanosis of the tongue

options.label: D
options.text: a bluish discoloration of the nail beds

options.label: E
options.text: jaundice from haem breakdown

questions.why: Carboxyhaemoglobin is bright red, so the skin looks cherry-red and cyanosis is absent despite tissue hypoxia.

questions.stem: The preferred treatment of significant carbon monoxide poisoning is

options.label: A
options.text: rebreathing into a closed paper bag

options.label: B
options.text: deliberate controlled hypoventilation

options.label: C
options.text: high-concentration or hyperbaric oxygen

options.label: D
options.text: an inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist

options.label: E
options.text: intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion

questions.why: High-concentration oxygen is the immediate treatment for significant carbon monoxide poisoning because it accelerates carbon monoxide elimination from haemoglobin and improves oxygen delivery. Hyperbaric oxygen may be considered in selected severe cases after specialist assessment.

notes.A: Closed-bag rebreathing reduces access to fresh oxygen and may worsen hypoxia, rather than accelerating displacement of carbon monoxide from haemoglobin.
notes.B: Hypoventilation limits oxygen delivery and elimination of inhaled carbon monoxide, opposing the treatment goal of rapid oxygenation and toxin clearance.
notes.D: Beta-2 agonists relieve bronchospasm but do not directly reverse carboxyhaemoglobin formation or replace the need for high-concentration oxygen.
notes.E: Sodium bicarbonate may have selected uses in acid–base management, but it does not directly displace carbon monoxide or replace oxygen treatment.

questions.stem: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane readily because they

options.label: A
options.text: dissolve first in a layer of water before diffusing

options.label: B
options.text: pass only through protein channels in the membrane

options.label: C
options.text: are carried across bound to surfactant

options.label: D
options.text: are lipid soluble and diffuse through the membrane directly

options.label: E
options.text: are actively pumped by alveolar type I cells

questions.why: Both gases are fat soluble and diffuse directly through the membrane rather than through water.

questions.stem: The diffusing capacity of the lung is greater for CO2 than for O2 — by about 20% — mainly because CO2 is

options.label: A
options.text: a smaller molecule than oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: carried entirely as bicarbonate

options.label: C
options.text: driven by a far larger partial-pressure gradient

options.label: D
options.text: unaffected by membrane thickness

options.label: E
options.text: much more soluble in the membrane fluids

questions.why: CO2's high solubility gives it a greater diffusing capacity despite its small partial-pressure gradient.

questions.stem: A lung unit with a ventilation/perfusion ratio of zero behaves as

options.label: A
options.text: a shunt, where alveolar gas resembles venous blood (PO2 ~40, PCO2 ~46)

options.label: B
options.text: pure dead space, where alveolar gas resembles inspired air

options.label: C
options.text: an ideal unit with perfect gas exchange

options.label: D
options.text: a unit with high O2 and no CO2

options.label: E
options.text: a region of maximal diffusing capacity

questions.why: V/Q = 0 means perfusion without ventilation (a shunt); the alveolar gas equilibrates toward venous values.

questions.stem: A lung unit with a ventilation/perfusion ratio approaching infinity has alveolar gas that

options.label: A
options.text: contains only residual-volume gas

options.label: B
options.text: resembles inspired air — high O2, very low CO2

options.label: C
options.text: resembles mixed venous blood — low O2, high CO2

options.label: D
options.text: has equal O2 and CO2 partial pressures

options.label: E
options.text: cannot exchange any gas with blood

questions.why: V/Q → ∞ means ventilation without perfusion (dead space); gas stays like inspired air (≈149 mmHg O2, ≈0 CO2).

questions.stem: Why is the lung apex, where V/Q is high, the site most prone to tuberculosis?

options.label: A
options.text: blood flow is greatest at the apex when upright

options.label: B
options.text: the airways there have the most cartilage

options.label: C
options.text: high local O2 with relatively poor perfusion

options.label: D
options.text: surfactant production is greatest there

options.label: E
options.text: intrapleural pressure is least negative there

questions.why: At the apex ventilation exceeds perfusion, so PO2 is high and flow low — conditions the tubercle bacillus favours.

questions.stem: Of the oxygen present in arterial blood, the proportion carried in simple solution in plasma is about

options.label: A
options.text: 50%, equally shared with haemoglobin

options.label: B
options.text: 20%, matching the inspired fraction

options.label: C
options.text: 10%, the remainder as bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: 1%, with roughly 99% bound to haemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: 30%, with the rest as carbamino compounds

questions.why: About 1% of blood O2 is dissolved; ~99% is combined with haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Rising from the first to the fourth oxygen molecule, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen

options.label: A
options.text: decreases progressively with each molecule bound

options.label: B
options.text: stays constant for all four sites

options.label: C
options.text: is highest for the first molecule

options.label: D
options.text: falls to zero once two sites are filled

options.label: E
options.text: increases progressively with each molecule bound

questions.why: Positive cooperativity means affinity rises as successive O2 molecules bind, until saturation flattens the curve.

questions.stem: Above an arterial PO2 of about 60 mmHg the dissociation curve is nearly flat, which means that

options.label: A
options.text: large rises in PO2 add little to the oxygen content of blood

options.label: B
options.text: oxygen content falls steeply with any rise in PO2

options.label: C
options.text: haemoglobin begins to release its oxygen rapidly

options.label: D
options.text: the blood is only half saturated

options.label: E
options.text: cooperative binding has not yet begun

questions.why: On the flat upper part, Hb is near fully saturated, so further PO2 rise adds little content — a safety margin for gas exchange.

questions.stem: The basic rhythm of quiet breathing is generated by neuron groups located in the

options.label: A
options.text: carotid body

options.label: B
options.text: medulla oblongata

options.label: C
options.text: cerebral cortex

options.label: D
options.text: hypothalamus

options.label: E
options.text: cervical spinal cord

questions.why: Medullary inspiratory and expiratory neuron groups set the automatic rhythm; the pons smooths it.

questions.stem: During quiet breathing the medullary expiratory neurons are largely silent because

options.label: A
options.text: the cortex overrides them at rest

options.label: B
options.text: CO2 levels are too low to excite them

options.label: C
options.text: expiration at rest is a passive elastic recoil

options.label: D
options.text: they are inhibited by the pneumotaxic centre

options.label: E
options.text: the vagus continuously suppresses them

questions.why: Quiet expiration is passive, so expiratory neurons discharge mainly during forced or increased breathing.

questions.stem: The pneumotaxic centre in the upper pons acts chiefly to

options.label: A
options.text: sense CO2 in the cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: B
options.text: drive forced expiration during exercise

options.label: C
options.text: trigger the cough reflex

options.label: D
options.text: limit inspiration and prevent sustained apneusis

options.label: E
options.text: generate the primary inspiratory drive

questions.why: The pneumotaxic centre switches off inspiration, preventing the sustained inspiratory cramp (apneusis).

questions.stem: Apneusis — sustained inspiratory spasm — appears when the brainstem is transected so as to remove the influence of the

options.label: A
options.text: medulla on the spinal motor neurons

options.label: B
options.text: cortex on the corticospinal tract

options.label: C
options.text: carotid bodies on the medulla

options.label: D
options.text: phrenic nerve on the diaphragm

options.label: E
options.text: pons and vagus on the inspiratory neurons

questions.why: Removing pontine (pneumotaxic) and vagal input leaves inspiration unchecked, producing apneusis.

questions.stem: Transection of the brainstem below the medulla has what effect on breathing?

options.label: A
options.text: breathing stops altogether

options.label: B
options.text: regular breathing continues unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: a gasping but rhythmic pattern persists

options.label: D
options.text: sustained inspiratory apneusis appears

options.label: E
options.text: only the cough reflex remains

questions.why: The respiratory drive originates in the medulla, so cutting below it abolishes breathing.

questions.stem: The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex limits over-inflation of the lung by means of

options.label: A
options.text: muscle spindles in the diaphragm

options.label: B
options.text: vagal stretch receptors that inhibit inspiration

options.label: C
options.text: chemoreceptors in the carotid body raising the rate

options.label: D
options.text: cortical impulses travelling down the corticospinal tract

options.label: E
options.text: J-receptors releasing surfactant

questions.why: Pulmonary stretch receptors send vagal afferents that inhibit the inspiratory neurons, ending inspiration when the lung is inflated.

questions.stem: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond most directly to

options.label: A
options.text: the plasma bicarbonate concentration

options.label: B
options.text: the temperature of the arterial blood

options.label: C
options.text: the H+ concentration of the cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: D
options.text: the arterial PO2 sensed at the carotid body

options.label: E
options.text: stretch of the pulmonary alveolar walls

questions.why: Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H+, which tracks arterial CO2 after CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier.

questions.stem: Arterial CO2 raises ventilation via the central chemoreceptors because CO2, unlike H+ and HCO3-,

options.label: A
options.text: binds directly to medullary neuron membranes

options.label: B
options.text: is detected only by the carotid bodies

options.label: C
options.text: lowers the pH of arterial plasma without entering the CSF

options.label: D
options.text: crosses the blood-brain barrier readily and generates H+ in the CSF

options.label: E
options.text: is actively pumped into the cerebrospinal fluid

questions.why: CO2 diffuses freely into the CSF and forms H+ there; H+ and HCO3- cross slowly, so CO2 is the effective central stimulus.

questions.stem: Afferent fibres from the carotid bodies reach the medulla through the

options.label: A
options.text: vagus nerve (cranial X)

options.label: B
options.text: trigeminal nerve (cranial V)

options.label: C
options.text: phrenic nerve (roots C3-C5)

options.label: D
options.text: facial nerve (cranial VII)

options.label: E
options.text: glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial IX)

questions.why: Carotid body afferents travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve; aortic body afferents travel in the vagus.

questions.stem: The peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated by dissolved oxygen lack, which is why they may fail to respond in

options.label: A
options.text: carbon monoxide poisoning

options.label: B
options.text: metabolic acidosis of any cause

options.label: C
options.text: ascent to high altitude

options.label: D
options.text: severe exercise with lactic acidosis

options.label: E
options.text: breath-holding to the breaking point

questions.why: They sense dissolved PO2; in CO poisoning dissolved O2 is near normal although Hb is saturated with CO, so they are poorly stimulated.

questions.stem: When inspired CO2 exceeds about 7%, alveolar PCO2 keeps rising despite hyperventilation and the subject develops

options.label: A
options.text: cheyne-stokes breathing from hypocapnia

options.label: B
options.text: CO2 narcosis with headache, confusion and coma

options.label: C
options.text: respiratory alkalosis with tetany

options.label: D
options.text: a leftward shift that improves O2 delivery

options.label: E
options.text: complete loss of chemoreceptor drive to O2

questions.why: Very high inspired CO2 produces hypercapnia that depresses the CNS — CO2 narcosis.

questions.stem: The breaking point of voluntary breath-holding is reached mainly because

options.label: A
options.text: alveolar O2 rises to a toxic level

options.label: B
options.text: the cortex loses control of the diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: rising CO2 and falling O2 force a breath

options.label: D
options.text: the lungs collapse once the residual volume is reached

options.label: E
options.text: the pneumotaxic centre is fatigued

questions.why: With no ventilation CO2 rises and O2 falls, and the resulting chemoreceptor drive forces a breath.

questions.stem: Giving a very low concentration of oxygen raises ventilation only weakly because the hyperventilation it causes

options.label: A
options.text: fatigues the carotid bodies within seconds

options.label: B
options.text: shifts the dissociation curve to the left

options.label: C
options.text: directly excites the pneumotaxic centre

options.label: D
options.text: washing out CO2, which inhibits breathing

options.label: E
options.text: at once raises arterial O2 back to normal

questions.why: Hypoxic hyperventilation blows off CO2; the hypocapnia opposes the drive, so only a very low PO2 overrides it.

questions.stem: In a patient with chronic CO2 retention whose drive to breathe has become dependent on hypoxia, the danger of giving 100% oxygen is that it may

options.label: A
options.text: cause an immediate respiratory alkalosis

options.label: B
options.text: trigger bronchospasm through cold air

options.label: C
options.text: precipitate carbon monoxide poisoning

options.label: D
options.text: shift the oxygen curve far to the right

options.label: E
options.text: remove the hypoxic drive and depress ventilation

questions.why: When the CO2 response is blunted, hypoxia is the main stimulus; abolishing it with high O2 can depress breathing.

questions.stem: The cough reflex is initiated by touch-sensitive receptors in the bronchi and trachea whose afferents travel in the

options.label: A
options.text: vagus nerve

options.label: B
options.text: glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: trigeminal nerve

options.label: D
options.text: phrenic nerve

options.label: E
options.text: facial nerve

questions.why: Tracheobronchial touch receptors send vagal afferents to the medulla to trigger coughing.

questions.stem: The sneeze reflex resembles the cough reflex but is triggered through the ___ nerve and directs air through the nose by depressing the uvula.

options.label: A
options.text: accessory

options.label: B
options.text: trigeminal

options.label: C
options.text: vagus

options.label: D
options.text: glossopharyngeal

options.label: E
options.text: hypoglossal

questions.why: Sneezing uses trigeminal (5th nerve) afferents from the nasal mucosa; the uvula is depressed to route air through the nose.

questions.stem: In the standard classification of hypoxia, 'anaemic hypoxia' means that

options.label: A
options.text: a toxin blocks the tissue's use of O2

options.label: B
options.text: oxygen cannot diffuse across the alveolar membrane

options.label: C
options.text: there is too little functional haemoglobin to carry O2

options.label: D
options.text: the arterial PO2 itself is reduced

options.label: E
options.text: blood flow to the tissue is too slow

questions.why: Anaemic hypoxia is inadequate O2 carriage from too little functional Hb; arterial PO2 is normal.

questions.stem: Cyanide poisoning produces which type of hypoxia?

options.label: A
options.text: anaemic hypoxia

options.label: B
options.text: stagnant hypoxia

options.label: C
options.text: anaemic hypoxia from CO

options.label: D
options.text: histotoxic hypoxia

options.label: E
options.text: hypoxic hypoxia

questions.why: Cyanide blocks the tissues' use of oxygen (cytochrome oxidase) — histotoxic hypoxia.

questions.stem: Slow blood flow, as in shock or heart failure, causes which type of hypoxia?

options.label: A
options.text: histotoxic hypoxia

options.label: B
options.text: hypoxic hypoxia

options.label: C
options.text: anaemic hypoxia

options.label: D
options.text: diffusion hypoxia

options.label: E
options.text: stagnant hypoxia

questions.why: When delivery is limited by sluggish flow despite normal blood and PO2, it is stagnant (ischaemic) hypoxia.

questions.stem: Clinically detectable cyanosis generally appears once the concentration of reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin reaches about

options.label: A
options.text: 5 g/dl

options.label: B
options.text: 1 g/dl

options.label: C
options.text: 10 g/dl

options.label: D
options.text: 15 g/dl

options.label: E
options.text: 2 g/dl

questions.why: About 5 g/dl of deoxyhaemoglobin is needed before the bluish colour is visible.

questions.stem: Severe anaemia rarely shows cyanosis even when the patient is hypoxic because

options.label: A
options.text: methaemoglobin masks the colour

options.label: B
options.text: too little Hb to give 5 g/dl of reduced Hb

options.label: C
options.text: the remaining haemoglobin is cherry red

options.label: D
options.text: arterial O2 is actually increased

options.label: E
options.text: the skin vessels are maximally dilated

questions.why: Cyanosis needs ~5 g/dl of deoxyHb; a severely anaemic patient simply lacks enough Hb to reach that level.

questions.stem: On rapid ascent to high altitude, the earliest compensatory response to the low inspired PO2 is

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in plasma pH from lactic acid

options.label: B
options.text: immediate polycythaemia

options.label: C
options.text: hyperventilation from chemoreceptor drive

options.label: D
options.text: a rise in red cell mass from erythropoietin

options.label: E
options.text: an increase in 2,3-DPG within hours

questions.why: Hypoxia stimulates the carotid/aortic bodies, producing prompt hyperventilation as the first step of acclimatization.

questions.stem: Over several days of acclimatization to altitude, a rise in 2,3-DPG is useful because it

options.label: A
options.text: raises the plasma bicarbonate directly

options.label: B
options.text: suppresses erythropoietin secretion

options.label: C
options.text: reduces the ventilatory response to hypoxia

options.label: D
options.text: shifts the curve rightward, making O2 more available to tissues

options.label: E
options.text: shifts the curve leftward, loading more O2 in the lungs

questions.why: Although alkalosis shifts the curve left, the accompanying rise in 2,3-DPG shifts it right, aiding tissue O2 delivery.

questions.stem: Erythropoietin released during acclimatization to altitude acts to

options.label: A
options.text: increase 2,3-DPG within minutes

options.label: B
options.text: stimulate the respiratory centre directly

options.label: C
options.text: cause immediate bronchodilatation

options.label: D
options.text: reduce plasma volume acutely

options.label: E
options.text: raise haemoglobin and red cell mass over a few days

questions.why: EPO rises with hypoxia and increases haemoglobin over 2–3 days, a key part of acclimatization.

questions.stem: Acute mountain sickness some hours after arrival at altitude is attributed partly to arteriolar dilatation that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes

options.label: A
options.text: cerebral and pulmonary oedema

options.label: B
options.text: bronchospasm and wheeze

options.label: C
options.text: methaemoglobinaemia

options.label: D
options.text: decompression bubbles in the joints

options.label: E
options.text: haemolysis of red cells

questions.why: Hypoxic arteriolar dilatation raises capillary pressure, leaking fluid into brain and lung — cerebral and pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: In a diver breathing compressed air, the narcotic effect producing euphoria and impaired judgement at depth is due to raised

options.label: A
options.text: water vapour pressure

options.label: B
options.text: nitrogen partial pressure

options.label: C
options.text: oxygen partial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: carbon dioxide partial pressure

options.label: E
options.text: helium partial pressure

questions.why: High PN2 at depth produces nitrogen narcosis with euphoria and clumsiness.

questions.stem: Decompression sickness ('the bends') on rapid ascent from a deep dive is caused by

options.label: A
options.text: rupture of alveoli from over-expansion

options.label: B
options.text: cold-induced bronchospasm

options.label: C
options.text: nitrogen bubbles coming out of solution

options.label: D
options.text: oxygen toxicity damaging the lungs

options.label: E
options.text: carbon dioxide retention in muscle

questions.why: Dissolved N2 forms bubbles if ascent is too fast, occluding vessels and causing joint pain, paraesthesiae and worse.

questions.stem: Breathing 100% oxygen for many hours is harmful partly because it

options.label: A
options.text: causes immediate nitrogen narcosis

options.label: B
options.text: raises plasma bicarbonate sharply

options.label: C
options.text: triggers the Hering-Breuer reflex

options.label: D
options.text: inhibits surfactant production and injures the airway

options.label: E
options.text: shifts the dissociation curve far to the right

questions.why: Prolonged high O2 irritates the airway, inhibits surfactant, kills lung macrophages and damages the lung within 1–2 days.

questions.stem: In a premature infant, prolonged high-concentration oxygen therapy can cause the eye complication

options.label: A
options.text: cataract from lens opacification

options.label: B
options.text: optic neuritis

options.label: C
options.text: central retinal artery occlusion

options.label: D
options.text: glaucoma

options.label: E
options.text: retrolental fibroplasia

questions.why: High O2 disrupts retinal vascular development, producing retrolental fibroplasia; broncho-pulmonary dysplasia affects the lungs.

questions.stem: During exercise the venous PO2 falls (for example from 40 toward 25 mmHg), which aids oxygenation in the lungs by

options.label: A
options.text: a wider alveolar-to-capillary O2 gradient

options.label: B
options.text: reducing the diffusing capacity of the membrane

options.label: C
options.text: raising alveolar PCO2 above arterial PCO2

options.label: D
options.text: closing dormant pulmonary capillaries

options.label: E
options.text: shifting the dissociation curve to the left

questions.why: Greater tissue extraction lowers mixed venous PO2, widening the gradient at the lung and increasing uptake.

questions.stem: In severe exercise an added chemical stimulus to the respiratory centre is

options.label: A
options.text: an increase in plasma bicarbonate

options.label: B
options.text: lactic acid that liberates CO2

options.label: C
options.text: a rise in arterial oxygen tension

options.label: D
options.text: a fall in core body temperature

options.label: E
options.text: a rise in red-cell 2,3-DPG alone

questions.why: Lactic acidosis in heavy exercise releases CO2 and lowers pH, stimulating ventilation.

questions.stem: A victim of fresh-water (hypotonic) near-drowning is at particular risk of

options.label: A
options.text: nitrogen narcosis

options.label: B
options.text: carbon monoxide poisoning

options.label: C
options.text: intravascular haemolysis of red cells

options.label: D
options.text: loss of plasma into the lungs causing shock

options.label: E
options.text: immediate decompression sickness

questions.why: Hypotonic fresh water is absorbed into the circulation and lyses red cells; sea water instead draws plasma into the lungs.

questions.stem: Hypocapnia from voluntary hyperventilation can cause tetany because the accompanying respiratory alkalosis

options.label: A
options.text: increases arterial PCO2

options.label: B
options.text: depresses the respiratory centre immediately

options.label: C
options.text: shifts the oxygen curve to the right

options.label: D
options.text: lowers ionised plasma calcium

options.label: E
options.text: raises ionised plasma calcium

questions.why: Alkalosis increases protein binding of calcium, lowering ionised Ca2+ and provoking tetany and paraesthesiae.

questions.stem: Asphyxia from airway occlusion combines low O2 with high CO2 and characteristically causes an early

options.label: A
options.text: fall in blood pressure with bradycardia

options.label: B
options.text: respiratory alkalosis

options.label: C
options.text: immediate loss of chemoreceptor activity

options.label: D
options.text: fall in circulating catecholamines

options.label: E
options.text: raised blood pressure and heart rate

questions.why: Asphyxia strongly drives respiration and sympathetic output, raising BP, heart rate and catecholamines before eventual collapse.
